newsitem.title: UK: Worried West looks on as Zaire lurches to collapse.
newsitem.headline: Worried West looks on as Zaire lurches to collapse.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
The collapse of Zaire could have profound and horrific consequences for Africa but the West will do little more than look on as the turmoil spreads, diplomats and analysts say.
The United States, Britain, France and former colonial power Belgium no longer have the strategic or economic interests that they once protected in Africa's third-largest country.
Nor are they in full agreement about what to do, diplomats say, beyond calling for an end to the fighting in Zaire and for neighbouring countries to stay out of the conflict.
President Mobutu Sese Seko, ill with cancer after ruling Zaire for more than 30 years, is trying to halt rebel advances with a ragged, demoralised army.

Neighbouring Rwanda and Uganda have backed the rebels, Western diplomats say, adding a dangerous international dimension to the conflict. Tens of thousands of refugees, many of whom fled neighbouring Rwanda in 1994, have been trapped by the fighting.

"The breakup of Zaire would have consequences for a whole swathe of Africa," said one Western diplomat involved with the region. "It could happen if Mobutu dies or the rebellion breaks up the country."
The human cost and the risks of instability spreading on the world's poorest continent are clear.

"Zaire matters a great deal but the notion of the West intervening to prop up a disintegrating state is far-fetched," said Professor Jack Spence of the Royal Institute of International Affairs (RIIA) in London.
Diplomats say memories are still fresh of the disastrous U.S.-led attempt to save another failing state, Somalia, in 1993. For that reason, Western intervention is extremely unlikely.
Plans were drawn up for a Canadian-led force to help refugees in eastern Zaire last year, but they were quickly dropped after many of the refugees -- although not all -- went home to Rwanda.
Outspoken critics like European Commissioner Emma Bonino have accused the big powers and the United Nations of abandoning their responsibilities.
Efforts by the United States and European countries to develop African peacekeeping mechanisms as a substitute have so far borne little fruit.

A senior Western diplomat dealing with the region said major powers were now struggling to keep other countries out of the conflict and to push for peace talks, as reflected in calls from the U.N. Security Council, the United States and others last week.

The problem is that Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila, buoyed up by his advances in eastern Zaire, is in no mood for compromise. His aim is to oust Mobutu, who seems equally determined to crush the uprising.
"If the government of Zaire believes there is a military solution they are probably going to preside over the break-up of Zaire," British aid minister Lynda Chalker said last week.
There have to be negotiations if there is not to be wholesale bloodshed in Zaire."
France, still a major power in Africa, and Belgium are particularly worried that the collapse of Mobutu's regime would threaten the borders, sovereignty and stability of other countries.

"Unlike Somalia...Zaire shares a border with nine other countries which will feel the effects of Zaire's ultimate destiny," the International Institute of Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a recent paper.
Most of them -- Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, Zambia, Angola, Congo and the Central African Republic -- already have major problems.
While France thinks there should be some support for Mobutu if it is the best way to hold Zaire together, the United States and Britain feel he has used up all of his credit with the West.
The U.S. ambassador to Kinshasa, Daniel Simpson, was quoted as saying recently that Zaire no longer had any importance or interest for Washington.
Mobutu was supported by Western governments during the Cold War but has been accused by human rights groups and others of massive abuses of power.

Zaire's vast mineral wealth, in diamonds and other materials, is still important although diplomats say years of instability and misrule mean that foreign commercial interests have been greatly reduced.
